assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new observational window built from a detector concept that was widely doubted: instrumenting a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice to catch high-energy astrophysical neutrinos. The diffuse flux, the 2018 TXS 0506+056 association, the NGC 1068 evidence and the Galactic-plane map open neutrino astronomy and bear directly on the origin of cosmic rays. This is the kind of instrument-driven discovery I value most, built on years of calibration and systematics work.
assessment.attribution: Halzen is the scientific driver and long-time principal investigator of IceCube and of its predecessor AMANDA. Spiering was a leading figure in the neutrino-telescope programme (Baikal, AMANDA, IceCube) and in its early history. Credit for a large collaboration is spread across many people, so this is a defensible but not unique pairing. Other leaders and the roles of the AMANDA and Baikal groups would need review.
assessment.maturity: Mature enough. The diffuse flux has been seen in several channels, and the source evidence has built up over about a decade. KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD provide partial independent context. The NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results are recent, but the central discovery of astrophysical neutrinos is secure.
uncertainties: Individual source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) have limited statistical significance and no independent confirmation from another detector.
I have not independently checked the precise roles of Halzen and Spiering against other IceCube and AMANDA founders.
A fair split of credit with a large collaboration is not obvious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle created the whole field of moiré quantum matter. The idea is original and clear, and it is now used well beyond graphene. This is outside my own expertise, so I would lean on the condensed-matter members.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive theoretical prediction in 2011. Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experiments. This is a clean theory plus experiment trio. Cao and others in the experimental group are not on the credited list, so I cannot name them.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced by many groups worldwide since 2018 across graphene, TMD and other moiré systems. Understanding of the superconductivity mechanism is still unsettled, but the discovery itself is stable. Timing is good.
uncertainties: The origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene remains debated.
Credit to the first author of the 2018 experiments and to earlier twistronics theory is unresolved within the supplied names.
I am relying on colleagues for the condensed-matter judgment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reaching 10^-18 fractional uncertainty are a real precision-measurement breakthrough. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea and Ye's group pushed the stability and accuracy. They enable tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The result rests on careful control of systematics, which I respect.
assessment.attribution: Katori conceived the optical lattice clock with magic wavelength trapping, and Ye led the demonstrations at the highest precision. The two-person configuration is clean. Ye also had a role in the frequency comb work recognised in 2005, but that does not hurt this claim.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) have built and compared lattice clocks. International comparisons confirm the claims. Timely, and the redefinition of the second may add further weight.
uncertainties: The relative weight of other optical clock platforms such as single-ion clocks is not captured by the credited names.
Whether the Committee would see this as incremental over the 2005 comb prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light now runs in the gravitational-wave detectors, improving their sensitivity. It is a clear case where a quantum-optics idea became a working detector technology and widened the observational reach of an existing prize-winning field. That connection to measurement instrumentation matters to me.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-state injection for interferometers in 1981. Kimble's group made early experimental demonstrations of squeezing. Schnabel led the GEO600 squeezed-light work and the implementation line. Mavalvala also made important contributions at LIGO. Other early experimentalists, for example in the Slusher group, are not on the list, so the configuration is somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing has been used routinely in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 since about 2019, and frequency-dependent squeezing was added later. The technology is well confirmed and the application is stable.
uncertainties: Early experimental squeezing credit is broader than the list and could be disputed.
Choosing three from four credited names leaves out Mavalvala, whose LIGO implementation role may be decisive in some views.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A* are direct visual evidence for black-hole shadows. They test general relativity in the strong-field regime. The achievement is a feat of instrumentation: a planet-sized VLBI array at 230 GHz with demanding calibration and imaging. It is a landmark, though a large part of the physics follows from the earlier black-hole prizes.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed imaging the shadow, Doeleman led the building of the array and the collaboration, and Moran contributed the long-baseline interferometry heritage. The work was done by a collaboration of hundreds, so a three-person attribution simplifies a lot. Other early leaders and key imaging-algorithm developers could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: The M87* image of 2019 was followed by Sgr A* in 2022 and later polarisation and multi-epoch data. Results are consistent but come from a single collaboration and instrument, so independent confirmation is limited. Interpretation, for example of the ring size and the spin, is still evolving.
uncertainties: No fully independent second instrument or analysis has repeated the images.
The prize-attribution problem for a very large collaboration is unresolved.
Physics novelty is more limited than the image impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kilonovae link neutron-star mergers to r-process nucleosynthesis and so address the origin of the heaviest elements. The multi-messenger event GW170817 gave a compelling case. The theory and the observation together have lasting impact on nuclear astrophysics and cosmology.
assessment.attribution: Lattimer and Schramm made the early prediction of ejecta from neutron-star mergers, Metzger and collaborators developed the kilonova model, and Kasen provided detailed radiative-transfer modelling. Tanvir reported the first kilonova candidate after GRB 130603B and was key to the 2017 observations. Observation credit in 2017 is shared by very many teams, so the allocation is complicated.
assessment.maturity: A single well-characterised event, GW170817, anchors the case, with other candidates after short GRBs. Evidence is strong that kilonovae produce r-process elements, but the share of heavy elements they contribute compared with other sites is not settled. Slightly premature without more events.
uncertainties: Only one clear multi-messenger event; the relative contribution to cosmic r-process abundances remains uncertain.
Lattimer's joint prediction with Schramm means a deceased co-originator is not eligible, which complicates the attribution.
Observational credit is spread across many teams.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magnetar model explains soft gamma repeaters and anomalous X-ray pulsars as neutron stars powered by decaying ultra-strong magnetic fields. It combined a clear prediction with confirmation by spin-down measurements. The 2020 Galactic magnetar flare tied to a fast radio burst raises the importance further. It is close to my own field of X-ray and gamma-ray instrumentation.
assessment.attribution: Duncan and Thompson made the 1992 theoretical prediction, and Kouveliotou's team measured the spin-down and field strength of SGR 1806-20 in 1998. A clean theory plus observation split. Paczynski, who proposed a related idea earlier, is deceased and not on the list.
assessment.maturity: The magnetar picture is widely accepted and has been confirmed by many objects and by outbursts. Some details, such as the persistent-emission mechanism and the link to FRBs, are still being worked out. The recognition is timely but may overlap strongly with other compact-object topics.
uncertainties: Alternative interpretations of some sources (for example fallback disks) were not fully excluded in the early period.
Related earlier theoretical ideas and the roles of other observers are not captured by the supplied names.
Link between magnetars and fast radio bursts is not yet settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping antiprotons and antihydrogen and measuring their properties directly tests CPT symmetry and the matter-antimatter asymmetry. These are heroic experiments of cooling, trapping and spectroscopy. As someone who has worked on cosmic-ray antimatter, I find the topic compelling, though null tests of symmetry give limited new physics so far.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led the trapping of antiprotons and antihydrogen with the ATRAP collaboration and made the precise antiproton and electron measurements. Hangst led ALPHA, which first trapped antihydrogen and made spectroscopic measurements. The two-person split is natural, although the ATHENA collaboration and others also contributed to producing cold antihydrogen.
assessment.maturity: ALPHA results on 1S-2S and other transitions and on gravity effects have been repeated and refined and are consistent with CPT. Independent confirmation exists in the ASACUSA and ATRAP work. The interpretation is stable, but the discovery content is limited by agreement with the Standard Model.
uncertainties: The prize-worthiness of null results versus a discovery is a question for the committee.
Credit for early cold-antihydrogen production (ATHENA) may be disputed.
I have not verified current precision levels beyond my general knowledge.
